summary: This program starts with a birthday party shopping list and then changes, adds, and removes items before printing the final list. It shows the four everyday list operations: replacing by index, appending, removing by value, and reading items back out.

lines.text: A list holds several values in one variable, in the order you wrote them. Square brackets create the list and commas separate the items.

lines.code: shopping_list[4] = "chouriço"  # Replace snacks with Portuguese sausage
lines.text: Lists are mutable, so you can overwrite a single position. Counting starts at 0, which makes index 4 the fifth item, "snacks".

lines.code: shopping_list.append("pastéis de nata")  # Portuguese custard tarts
lines.text: The append method adds one new item to the end of the list, growing it from seven items to eight.
Unlike indexing, remove searches for a matching value and deletes the first one it finds, so you do not need to know the position.
A heading printed before the loop makes the output readable rather than a bare column of words.
A for loop visits each element in turn, storing it in the variable item so the body can work with one value at a time.
The indentation marks this line as the loop body, and passing two arguments to print puts a dash and a space in front of each item.
Index 0 is always the first element. The \n prints a blank line first, and the f prefix lets you drop an expression straight into the text inside braces.
Negative indexes count backwards from the end, so -1 reliably gives the last item even after the list has changed size.
